title: How Companies Assess Fit of Engineers on a Behavioral Interview
author: Gregor Ojstersek and Steve Huynh
summary: Guest author Steve Huynh, a former Amazon Principal Engineer and Bar Raiser who conducted nearly 1,000 interviews, explains what companies are really evaluating in the behavioral interview. Technical interviews only check the box on skills, he says, while behavioral interviews decide role fit, company fit, and the level at which a candidate would be hired. Because candidates cannot simply be asked whether they fit, interviewers read signals in the stories candidates tell. Huynh walks through seven common mis-fits, such as independent versus collaborative work, shipping fast versus being thorough, and direct versus diplomatic communication, to show that the same behavior can be a strength at one company and a liability at another. He then lays out four dimensions that determine level, namely scope, contribution, impact, and difficulty, with expectations from entry level through principal. The practical lesson is to choose stories that match what the target company and role value.
points: Technical skill only clears the first gate; behavioral interviews decide whether you fit the role and company and what level you are offered.
Interviewers infer fit from signals in your stories, so the same story can read as quality-minded at one company and as analysis paralysis at another.
Huynh's seven mis-fit examples show that traits like speed, independence, directness, and data-orientation are culture-dependent rather than universally good.
Level is judged across scope, contribution, impact, and difficulty, so a strong story must show how many people it affected, what you personally did, what changed, and how hard the problem was.
Candidates should work backwards from the company's values and select stories that demonstrate those specific qualities.
quotes: Companies can’t just directly ask: “Would you fit here”? Because, I don’t believe any candidate would answer the question with “No”.
Instead, what companies do, is look for signals in your stories that show either you are a fit or not.
You spending 3 weeks perfecting a solution might demonstrate attention to quality at one company but analysis paralysis at another.
Moving fast and fixing issues later demonstrates good judgment at a growth startup but recklessness at an established healthcare company.
If all your stories are about going off and building something by yourself, consensus-driven companies will worry that you’ll steamroll people or make decisions without informing anyone.
Contribution captures what you did, not what happened around you. It is important to be precise about the line between “I” and “we.
Under this category, solving easy problems with big impacts is less impressive than hard problems solved well.
Companies aren’t just evaluating whether you can do the job. They’re also assessing whether you’ll thrive in their specific environment and at what level you’ll be most effective.
